title: Lina and the Whispering Pine
markdown:
Consider this quiet little corner of the world, the Northwind Heights, where tall pine trees reach for the clouds and their needles make a soft tinkling song when the wind blows. In this special place lived a young elf named Lina. Eyes like smooth grey stones, full of quiet wonder. She loved quiet moments, especially when the sky turned soft pink and purple at dusk. Her very best friend was not a bunny or a squirrel. It was a crow. A very busy crow named Corvus. Feathers as dark and shiny as a polished pebble. Chatter as bright and happy as the first star at night.

One night the moon was a pale thin curve, casting long dancing shadows through the tinkling pinewood. Trees seemed to whisper secrets. Lina walked with Corvus on her shoulder, tiny claws a steady comforting weight. He often pointed: “Caw! Look, Lina! A fuzzy green patch! Or a shiny drop of water!” And Lina, with a little smile, would always look.

Tonight a little question stirred. “Corvus,” soft as falling snow, “I have something important to ask the old Pine Tree.”

The old Pine Tree was a truly grand sight, right in the middle of the woods, branches like big kind arms to the starry sky. It was said to know all the secrets of the Northwind Heights, all the quiet wonders.

“A question?” Head tilt, bright black eye twinkling. “What kind? Where the juiciest bugs hide? Why the clouds move so slowly?”

Lina giggled, tiny bells. “Oh, no. A very quiet question. A question about a feeling that sometimes tickles inside me, like a secret wish.” She patted the pocket of her little shirt, where she kept a smooth grey stone from the whispering stream. This question felt important.

Deeper in, a wonderful smell: warm, sweet, a little spicy, like sunshine baked into a perfect golden treat. Corvus puffed his chest. “My, my. That smells like pure joy.”

Around a gentle bend, tucked among sweet-smelling firs: a small cozy cottage, a puff of smoke. Beside it, laying out rows of golden pastries, a round rosy-cheeked goblin, flour on his cheerful nose and apron like a soft blanket of snow. Gnorman the goblin baker. Everyone in the Heights knew him for his comforting treats.

“Well, hello there, little travellers! Who might you be, out so late in the whispering woods?”

“I’m Lina. And this is my friend, Corvus. We’re going to ask the old Pine Tree a question.” A little bow.

A chuckle like happy pebbles. “The Pine Tree, eh? A wise choice. It’s seen more seasons than any of us can count. But before you go, would you like to try one of my Moonbeam Muffins? Just out of the oven. They taste like sleepy clouds drifting on a summer day.”

Lina’s eyes grew wide. Corvus, who never said no to a treat, flapped with delight. “Sleepy clouds?” Hop on the shoulder.

Gnorman gave Lina a muffin, warm and soft. Vanilla and honey, a hint of cinnamon that made her nose wiggle. The quiet secret feeling inside her felt even warmer. “Oh, thank you. It’s so, so good.” A little muffled.

Gnorman wiped floury hands. He did not tell her that trees remember stories. He only nodded toward the dark strong shape against the stars. “Sometimes the oldest trees don’t need to say their answers out loud. Just seeing them stand tall, through every kind of weather… that can be the answer.”

Lina paused, muffin halfway. The Pine Tree didn’t say a single word. Branches rustled, a gentle sighing that seemed to understand. Needles tinkled. All is well, little one. You are here. You are safe. Or perhaps that was only Lina, hearing what she had come to ask.

Corvus nudged her cheek. “The muffin was a very good answer, too.” A little wink.

She smiled all the way to her kind eyes. Gnorman’s words, the quiet steady pine, Corvus’s weight: the ticklish feeling felt not just warm, but wonderfully safe. Exactly where she belonged.

“Thank you, Gnorman. And thank you, old Pine Tree.”

With Corvus snuggled on her shoulder, and the sweet smell of baking lingering like a happy memory, Lina turned home. She saved the last muffin crumb for the walk, and Corvus pretended not to notice, then noticed. The pinewood tinkled a soft goodbye. Moonbeams like a gentle silver path, perfectly safe, perfectly bright, perfectly hers. The grey stone stayed in her pocket, warmer now from being held. The question, for tonight, had been asked enough.
